newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Italy, Spain face new year troubles.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Italy, Spain face new year troubles.

text.p: Italian and Spanish bonds will continue to outclass their German counterparts, riding a wave of positive sentiment to the end of 1996, analysts said on Tuesday.
But the risk that external upsets will jolt "Club Med" bond holders back to reality in the new year is high, with yield spreads threatening to bloat again.
"In the short term the outlook is quite positive," said Ken Wattret, international economist at Paribas Capital Markets in London. "The momentum is still there and spreads could narrow even further."
While Italian bonds have slowed the pace of outperformance in the past few weeks, the BTP/Bund yield gap is still narrowing, trading at 173 basis points now in comparison with 500 a year ago.
In Spain the 10-year Bono/Bund yield gap snapped to its lowest ever level at 120 basis points on Tuesday, down from just over 400 basis points this time last year.

Analysts said the prospect for interest rate cuts in Spain and Italy before 1996 draws to a close, coupled with falling inflation and continued convergence towards the single currency Maastricht criteria, should provide support in the short term.
But they said the froth at the top of the markets was in danger of being wiped away as 1997 begins.
"I'd be a bit cautious about these markets at current levels," said Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ International in London.
The risk, analysts said, was that a change in sentiment at the start of next year would force yield spreads back up.
"Domestic events, especially in Italy, will compound any sell-off in the first half of next year," said Wattret.

"But the trigger is likely to come from outside -- the key will be what happens to economic activity in Germany and whether interest rates will start to rise towards the middle of the year. That will lead to a sea change in market sentiment on European bonds in general."
But Phyllis Reed, European bond strategist at BZW in London, said investors should not be tempted into panic selling when the turn comes about.

"Next year people will probably reassess the ability of Italy and Spain to get into the single European currency in the first round (in 1999), but that does not mean we will see a big unwinding of the convergence trades," she said.
"We wouldn't want to be big sellers."
Reed pointed to two major factors which she said meant spreads around the 500 basis point mark, which used to characterise BTP and Bonos, would probably never be seen again.
"The convergence in the first half of the year was achieved in a bear market. That is unusual and it indicates that the convergence is much more sustainable," she said.
While U.S. bond yields rose around 100 basis points in the first half of this year, both Spanish and Italian spreads to Bunds fell by as much as that and more.
Another supporting factor is the wealth of domestic money behind the two markets, analysts said, suggesting that any sell-off should be more of a considered correction than a sharp slide.
"It tends to be the markets heavily held by international investors that get hit hardest when we start to run into troubles," said Reed.
IBJ's Edmonds agreed. He forecast the BTP/Bund spread would puff out to 190 in the next three months but would return to 150 basis points by the end of 1997.
Bonos too, will underperform in the first quarter of 1997, pushing the yield gap to Bunds out to 140 basis points, before converging again to around 100 by the end of the year.
-- Kate Kelland, International Bonds Unit +44 171 542 8682
